text: The tallest person in recorded history was Robert Wadlow of Alton, Illinois, who reached 2.72 meters (8 ft 11.1 in) at the time of his death in 1940.
The shortest adult in recorded history was Chandra Bahadur Dangi of Nepal, who measured 54.6 cm (1 ft 9.5 in) when verified by Guinness World Records in 2012.
The world's deepest ocean point is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at approximately 10,935 meters below sea level.
Mount Everest is the world's highest peak above sea level at 8,848.86 meters, as re-measured by a China-Nepal joint survey in 2020.
The fastest wind speed ever recorded was 408 km/h (253 mph), measured during Tropical Cyclone Olivia on Barrow Island, Australia on April 10, 1996.
The hottest air temperature ever recorded was 56.7°C (134°F) at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, California on July 10, 1913.
The coldest naturally occurring temperature on Earth was -89.2°C (-128.6°F), recorded at Vostok Station, Antarctica on July 21, 1983.
The largest living organism on Earth is a honey fungus (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon's Malheur National Forest, covering 9.65 km² and estimated to be 8,000 years old.
The fastest land animal is the cheetah, capable of reaching speeds of up to 112 km/h (70 mph) in short bursts of up to 500 meters.
The peregrine falcon holds the record for the fastest animal on Earth, diving at speeds exceeding 389 km/h (242 mph) during its hunting stoop.
The blue whale is the largest animal ever known to have existed on Earth, reaching lengths of up to 33 meters and weighing up to 200 tonnes.
The world's oldest living tree is a Great Basin bristlecone pine named Methuselah in California's White Mountains, estimated to be over 4,850 years old.
The world's longest recorded flight by a bird was made by a bar-tailed godwit that flew 13,560 km nonstop from Alaska to Australia in 11 days in 2022.
The world's heaviest rideable bicycle weighs 750 kg and was built by Wouter van den Bosch of the Netherlands in 2010.
The current 100-meter sprint world record is 9.58 seconds, set by Usain Bolt of Jamaica at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin.
The women's 100-meter world record is 10.49 seconds, set by Florence Griffith-Joyner of the United States at the 1988 US Olympic Trials in Indianapolis.
The world's tallest building is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, UAE, at 828 meters (2,717 feet), with 163 floors above ground.

source.name: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat

text: The longest recorded successful sniper shot was made by a Canadian soldier in Iraq in 2017 at a range of 3,540 meters, using a McMillan TAC-50 rifle.
The heaviest weight ever lifted by a human was 2,844 kg (6,270 lbs), recorded as a backlift by Paul Anderson of the USA in 1957.
The world's fastest rollercoaster is the Formula Rossa at Ferrari World Abu Dhabi, reaching 240 km/h (149 mph) in just 4.9 seconds.
The longest marathon ever run was completed by Yiannis Kouros of Greece, who ran 1,000 miles in 10 days, 10 hours, 30 minutes, and 35 seconds in 1988.
The current men's marathon world record is 2 hours, 0 minutes, 35 seconds, set by Kelvin Kiptum of Kenya at the 2023 Chicago Marathon.
The deepest scuba dive was achieved by Ahmed Gabr of Egypt in 2014, reaching a depth of 332.35 meters in the Red Sea.
The world's largest pizza ever made was a gluten-free pizza measuring 1,261.65 m² (13,580.7 sq ft), created in Rome, Italy in 2012.
The heaviest carrot ever grown weighed 10.17 kg (22.44 lbs), grown by Christopher Qualley in the USA and verified in 2017.
The world's oldest confirmed living human was Jeanne Calment of France, who died in 1997 at age 122 years and 164 days.
The loudest sound ever produced by a human was 129 dB at 1 meter, set by Annalisa Flanagan of the UK in 1994.
The Nile is the longest river in the world at approximately 6,650 km, flowing north through 11 countries before emptying into the Mediterranean Sea.
The Amazon River carries more water than the next seven largest rivers combined, discharging approximately 209,000 cubic meters of fresh water into the ocean per second.
The world record for holding one's breath underwater is 24 minutes and 37 seconds, set by Budimir Šobat of Croatia in 2021.
The longest fingernails ever on a pair of hands belonged to Lee Redmond of the USA, whose nails measured a combined length of 8.65 meters in 2008.
The world's largest desert is Antarctica, a cold desert covering 14.2 million km²—nearly twice the size of the Sahara, the world's largest hot desert.
The Sahara Desert is the world's largest hot desert, covering 9.2 million km² across 11 African countries, roughly the size of the contiguous United States.
The highest recorded score in a single game of Pac-Man is 3,333,360 points (a perfect score), achieved by Billy Mitchell of the USA on July 3, 1999.
The most gold medals won at a single Olympics was by swimmer Michael Phelps at the 2008 Beijing Games, where he won eight gold medals—all in individual and relay events.
Michael Phelps is the most decorated Olympian of all time with 28 medals total (23 gold, 3 silver, 2 bronze) across four Olympic Games.
The most points scored in an NBA game by a single player was 100 points by Wilt Chamberlain for the Philadelphia Warriors against the New York Knicks on March 2, 1962.
The Three Gorges Dam in China is the world's largest hydroelectric dam by total generating capacity, producing up to 22,500 megawatts.
The Great Wall of China is the world's longest wall and human-made structure, stretching over 21,196 km including all its sections, branches, and tributaries.
The world record for the most Big Mac hamburgers eaten is 32,672, by Donald Gorske of Wisconsin, who has eaten at least one Big Mac daily since 1972.
The world's longest unassisted climb of a sheer rock face was Alex Honnold's free solo ascent of El Capitan's Freerider route in 3 hours 56 minutes on June 3, 2017.
The largest snowflake ever recorded was reportedly 38 cm (15 in) wide and 20 cm (8 in) thick, observed in Fort Keogh, Montana, USA on January 28, 1887.
The world's highest waterfall is Angel Falls in Venezuela, with a total drop of 979 meters (3,212 ft), nearly 20 times taller than Niagara Falls.
The fastest goal in professional soccer was scored by Nawaf Al-Abed of Saudi Arabia after just 2.4 seconds in a match in 2009.
The world's most expensive painting is Leonardo da Vinci's Salvator Mundi, which sold at Christie's New York in November 2017 for $450.3 million.
The largest recorded earthquake in history was a magnitude 9.5 (Mw) megathrust earthquake in Valdivia, Chile on May 22, 1960, felt as far away as Japan and Hawaii.
The world's largest ocean is the Pacific, which covers approximately 165 million km²—larger than all of Earth's landmasses combined.
The men's high jump world record is 2.45 meters, set by Javier Sotomayor of Cuba on July 27, 1993, in Salamanca, Spain—a record that has stood for over 30 years.
The world's most venomous snake is the inland taipan of Australia; a single bite contains enough venom to kill 100 adult humans.
The world record for the most holes of golf played in 24 hours is 420 holes, set by Ian Colston of Australia in 1971 at Bendigo Golf Club.
The longest individual world chess championship match was the 1984–85 Karpov vs Kasparov match, which was abandoned after 48 games with no decisive result over five months.
The world's largest human mosaic was created in the UAE in 2015, consisting of 30,000 volunteers forming the image of the UAE flag in celebration of the country's 44th National Day.
Lake Baikal in Russia is the world's deepest lake at 1,642 meters and holds approximately 22–23% of the world's fresh surface water.
The fastest recorded tennis serve was 263.4 km/h (163.7 mph), hit by Sam Groth of Australia at the 2012 Busan Open Challenger Tennis in South Korea.
The world's fastest human to walk 100 km was Yiannis Kouros of Greece, who completed the distance in 7 hours 25 minutes and 47 seconds in 2009.
The highest altitude skydive was Felix Baumgartner's 2012 jump from 39,045 meters above Earth, during which he broke the sound barrier at 1,357.64 km/h.
The world's largest gathering of people in a single location was the Kumbh Mela in Allahabad, India in 2013, where an estimated 30 million pilgrims gathered in a single day.
The world's largest known cave is Son Doong Cave in Quang Binh Province, Vietnam, with a main passage over 9 km long, 200 meters high, and 150 meters wide.
The men's pole vault world record is 6.21 meters, set by Armand Duplantis of Sweden in 2024, breaking his own previous record for the ninth time.
The world's longest bone in the human body is the femur (thigh bone), which makes up roughly a quarter of a person's total height.
The deepest borehole ever drilled is the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, reaching 12,262 meters deep over 24 years of drilling before being abandoned in 1994.
The world's largest diamond ever found was the Cullinan diamond, discovered in South Africa in 1905; it weighed 3,106.75 carats in its rough form.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

text: The world's fastest growing plant is bamboo, with some species growing up to 91 cm (36 inches) in a single 24-hour period under ideal conditions.
The world's largest gold nugget, the Welcome Stranger, was found in Victoria, Australia in 1869; it weighed 71.014 kg (156 lbs 10 oz) gross.
The fastest hat-trick in professional soccer was scored by Tommy Ross of Ross County in just 90 seconds against Nairn County on November 28, 1964.
The longest time anyone has survived without food is 382 days, achieved by Angus Barbieri of Scotland in 1965–66 under medical supervision, losing 125 kg.
The world's heaviest hailstone ever recorded weighed 1.02 kg (2.25 lbs) and fell in Gopalganj District, Bangladesh on April 14, 1986.
The most tries scored in a Rugby World Cup was by Jonah Lomu of New Zealand, who scored 15 tries across two tournaments (1995 and 1999).
The world's heaviest fruit is a pumpkin; the record was set in 2021 when Stefano Cutrupi of Italy grew one weighing 1,226 kg (2,702 lbs).
The world's most abundant element in the universe is hydrogen, making up about 75% of all normal (baryonic) matter by mass.
The most Grand Slam tennis singles titles won by any player is 24, held by Novak Djokovic of Serbia as of 2023, surpassing the previous records held by Federer, Nadal, and Williams.
The world's highest volcanic eruption column was from the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines, which reached an altitude of 40 km.
The world record for the most languages spoken fluently by one person is 58 languages, claimed by Ziad Fazah of Lebanon, born in 1954, though this is disputed.
The largest snowman ever built was 37.21 meters tall, named Olympia SnowWoman, constructed in Bethel, Maine, USA in February 2008.
The world's largest lake by surface area is the Caspian Sea, covering 371,000 km², which is classified as a lake because it is fully landlocked.
The fastest swim across the English Channel was 6 hours, 55 minutes, set by Trent Grimsey of Australia on September 8, 2012.
The most books written by one author is 1,075, credited to Brazilian author Ryoki Inoue, who wrote under 39 different pen names across multiple genres.
The world's highest tides occur in the Bay of Fundy between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, Canada, where tidal ranges can exceed 16 meters (53 feet).
The world's fastest recorded punch was 45 mph (72 km/h), thrown by boxer Keith Liddell, who holds the Guinness record for the world's fastest punch.
The world's oldest known living animal is a Greenland shark estimated to be 392 years old, making it older than the United States, calculated by radiocarbon dating of its eye lens.
The world record for the most rotations on a balance board in one minute is 91, set by Sanket Shelar of India in 2019.
The longest baseball game in professional history lasted 33 innings between the Pawtucket Red Sox and Rochester Red Wings on April 18–19, 1981, finally ending after 8 hours and 25 minutes of play.
The world record for eating hot dogs is 76 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes, set by Joey Chestnut of the USA at the 2021 Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest.
The world's most powerful earthquake instrumentally recorded was the 1960 Valdivia earthquake (magnitude 9.5), which triggered tsunamis affecting Chile, Hawaii, Japan, and the Philippines.
The world's most decorated military person was Audie Murphy of the United States, who received 33 decorations including the Medal of Honor during World War II.
The fastest guitar playing record is 1,600 beats per minute, set by Dr. Hot Licks (John Taylor) of the UK in 2012, playing the Flight of the Bumblebee.
The world record for running the most marathons in a year is 365 marathons in 365 days, completed by Arun Bhardwaj of India in 2020.
The world's largest iceberg ever recorded was B-15, which broke off the Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica in 2000, measuring 295 km long and 37 km wide—larger than Jamaica.

source.name: National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: The most consecutive free throws in an NBA game by a team was 39, set by the Cleveland Cavaliers against the Golden State Warriors on February 20, 2009.
The world's largest wave ever surfed was 26.21 meters (86 ft), ridden by Sebastian Steudtner of Germany at Nazaré, Portugal on October 29, 2020.
The world's fastest ant is the Saharan silver ant (Cataglyphis bombycina), capable of running at 855 mm/s—proportionally faster than a cheetah relative to body length.
The world's longest bridge between two countries is the Crimean Bridge (Kerch Bridge), at 19 km connecting Russia to the Crimean Peninsula over the Kerch Strait.
The world record for the most pushups in 24 hours is 46,001, set by Charles Servizio of the USA in 1993.
The wettest place on Earth is Mawsynram in Meghalaya, India, which receives an average annual rainfall of 11,873 mm (467 inches).
The tallest sandcastle ever built measured 21.16 meters and was constructed in Binz, Germany in 2019 by a team of sculptors from around the world.

The most wins at the Tour de France by a single rider is 7, achieved by both Lance Armstrong (later stripped due to doping) and now standing at 5 for Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, Miguel Indurain, and Jacques Anquetil.
The most runs scored in a single innings in Test cricket was 952 for 6 declared, by Sri Lanka against India in Colombo in 1997.
The world's largest swimming pool by surface area is the San Alfonso del Mar pool in Algarrobo, Chile, stretching 1,013 meters and holding 250 million liters of water.
The fastest time to climb Mount Everest from base camp is 10 hours 56 minutes and 46 seconds, set by Lhakpa Gelu Sherpa of Nepal in 2003.
The largest confirmed meteorite ever found is the Hoba meteorite in Namibia, weighing approximately 60 tonnes and measuring 2.7 × 2.7 meters; it has never been moved from its discovery site.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

text: The world's oldest cheese, about 3,200 years old, was found in 2018 in an ancient Egyptian tomb at Saqqara, making it the oldest solid cheese ever discovered.
The fastest anyone has ever spoken in a public speech was 637 words per minute, achieved by Steve Woodmore of the UK in 1990.
The most expensive spice in the world by weight is saffron, which costs up to $5,000 per pound; it takes about 75,000 saffron flowers to produce one pound of the spice.
The deepest lake in the world not counting Lake Baikal's 1,642-meter maximum is Lake Tanganyika in Africa at 1,470 meters deep—the second deepest in the world.
The most prolific female athlete in the Olympics is gymnast Larisa Latynina of the Soviet Union, who won 18 Olympic medals (9 gold, 5 silver, 4 bronze) from 1956 to 1964.
The longest winning streak in professional sports was achieved by the New Zealand All Blacks rugby team, winning 18 consecutive test matches from 2015 to 2016.
The longest winning streak in tennis Grand Slams was 23 consecutive Grand Slam titles by Steffi Graf, who won all four Grand Slams in 1988 plus the Olympic gold—the Golden Slam.
The most expensive house ever sold was the Villa Les Cèdres in Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat, France, sold in 2020 for approximately €350 million.
The longest continuous rainfall event ever recorded lasted 331 days at Big Bog on Maui, Hawaii, receiving over 10,300 mm (406 inches) of rain in that period.
The most goals scored in a career by a male soccer player is 819 official goals, achieved by Cristiano Ronaldo of Portugal as of 2023, surpassing Josef Bican's previous record.
The world's most venomous spider is the Sydney funnel-web spider; its venom can kill a human in 15 minutes if untreated, though an antivenom developed in 1980 has eliminated fatalities in Australia.
The most stitches in a quilt used in a record is 1,799,500, achieved by members of the Temecula Valley Quilt Guild in California over several years.
The tallest active geyser on Earth is Steamboat Geyser in Yellowstone National Park, which can shoot water up to 90 meters (300 feet) in the air during major eruptions.
The world's largest living bird by weight is the common ostrich, which can weigh up to 156 kg (344 lbs) and stands up to 2.8 meters tall.
The smallest bird in the world is the bee hummingbird of Cuba, measuring just 5.7 cm (2.24 in) in length and weighing about 1.95 grams.
The most expensive coffee in the world is Kopi Luwak, made from beans eaten and passed through the digestive system of Asian palm civets, selling for up to $700 per kg.
The most expensive bottle of whisky ever sold was a 1926 Macallan 'Fine and Rare,' which fetched $1.9 million at Sotheby's in 2019.
The world's oldest known recipe is a Sumerian beer recipe engraved on a clay tablet dating to approximately 1800 BCE.
The most powerful nuclear weapon ever detonated was the Soviet Tsar Bomba on October 30, 1961, with a yield of 50 megatons—3,300 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb.
The world's fastest time to solve a Rubik's Cube is 3.13 seconds, set by Max Park of the USA at the 2023 Pride in Long Beach competition.
The largest volcanic eruption in recorded history was Mount Tambora in Indonesia in 1815, which ejected 150–180 km³ of material and caused the 'Year Without a Summer' in 1816.
The world's fastest production motorcycle is the Kawasaki Ninja H2R, which can reach a top speed of approximately 400 km/h (249 mph) on a closed track.
The world record for the longest swim in open ocean was set by Martin Strel of Slovenia, who swam the entire length of the Amazon River—5,268 km—in 66 days in 2007.
The oldest message in a bottle was found in 2018 in Western Australia; it had drifted for 131 years and 223 days after being thrown overboard from a German ship in 1886.
The most expensive commercial real estate in the world per square meter is in Hong Kong, where some office properties exceed $50,000 per square meter.
The most touchdowns scored in an NFL career is 208 rushing touchdowns by Emmitt Smith of the Dallas Cowboys, who also holds the record for career rushing yards at 18,355.
The largest stadium in the world is the Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in Pyongyang, North Korea, with a seating capacity of 114,000.
The world's loudest animal relative to its body size is the water boatman insect (Micronecta scholtzi), which produces sounds of up to 99.2 dB using a structure on its genitalia.
The most expensive car ever sold at auction was a 1962 Ferrari 250 GTO, which fetched $48.4 million at RM Sotheby's in August 2018.
The longest tennis match in history lasted 11 hours and 5 minutes over three days at Wimbledon 2010, when John Isner defeated Nicolas Mahut 70-68 in the fifth set.

The world's largest waterfall by volume of water is the underwater Denmark Strait Cataract, which drops 3,505 meters (11,500 ft) between Greenland and Iceland—over three times taller than Angel Falls.
The world's lightest solid material is aerogel, which can be as light as 1 mg/cm³, is 99.8% air, and holds 15 Guinness World Records for various material properties.
The most wins in Formula One is 103 races, held by Lewis Hamilton of the UK, who also holds the records for most pole positions (104) and most podium finishes.
The world's oldest university still in operation is the University of Bologna in Italy, founded in 1088 CE.
The most durable marathon runner ever was Fauja Singh, who ran his last marathon at age 101 at the Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2011, finishing in 8 hours and 25 minutes.

The world's most goals scored by a team in a single association football match was 149-0, when AS Adema beat Stade Olympique de L'Emyrne in Madagascar in 2002 (the losing team intentionally scored own goals in protest).
The world's lowest natural point on dry land is the Dead Sea shore in Jordan and Israel, at approximately 430 meters (1,412 feet) below sea level.
The most expensive auction lot ever sold was a single painting: Salvator Mundi by Leonardo da Vinci, at $450.3 million in November 2017 at Christie's New York.
The most goals scored in a single FIFA World Cup is 13, by Just Fontaine of France in the 1958 tournament in Sweden—a record that has stood for over 65 years.
The longest confirmed lifespan of any vertebrate animal is the ocean quahog clam, with one individual ('Ming') found to be 507 years old based on growth ring counting.
The world record for most chin-ups in one minute is 57, set by Flexmaster UK in 2021, while the record for the most in one hour is 993 by Stephen Hyland of the UK.
The world's tallest volcano is Mauna Kea in Hawaii; though its summit is only 4,205 meters above sea level, its total height from the ocean floor is 10,210 meters—taller than Everest.
The world's most expensive mushroom is the white truffle (Tuber magnatum), with record prices exceeding $5,000 per 100 grams at auction; a 1.51 kg truffle sold for $330,000 in 2007.
The most hat-tricks scored in NHL history is 50, by Wayne Gretzky of Canada, who also holds over 60 other NHL records including 2,857 career points.
The oldest surviving wine in the world is the Speyer wine, a bottle of Roman wine discovered in a tomb in Germany in 1867, dating from around 325 CE.
The fastest time to run a mile is 3 minutes 43.13 seconds, set by Hicham El Guerrouj of Morocco in Rome on July 7, 1999—a record that has stood for over 25 years.
The greatest recorded snowfall in 24 hours was 193 cm (76 inches) at Silver Lake, Colorado on April 14–15, 1921.
The world record for most International cricket centuries (100+ runs) is 100, achieved by Sachin Tendulkar of India across all formats of the game.
The world's fastest bird in level flight is the common swift, which has been recorded flying at 111.6 km/h (69.3 mph) in level flight during the breeding season.
The world's largest living structure is the Great Barrier Reef off Queensland, Australia, stretching over 2,300 km and visible from space—it is made up of over 2,900 individual reefs.

source.name: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

text: The greatest number of World Cup wins by a national soccer team is 5, held by Brazil (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002).
The world's longest coastline belongs to Canada, with 202,080 km of coastline including islands—more than 25 times the circumference of the Earth.
The largest human pyramid ever assembled consisted of 10 tiers and 280 people, achieved by BRISKO Estefanio in India on November 6, 2014.
The most expensive jewel ever sold at auction is the CTF Pink Star diamond, a 59.60-carat pink diamond that sold for $71.2 million at Sotheby's Hong Kong in April 2017.
The world's largest hot spring is the Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone, measuring 91 meters deep and 113 meters wide, with vivid rainbow-colored microbial mats around its edges.
The most tennis aces served in a single match is 113, hit by Ivo Karlović of Croatia against Alessandro Proto at the 2015 Davis Cup—a record for any professional match.
The largest organism ever measured by area (a clonal colony) is Pando, a quaking aspen grove in Utah covering 43 hectares, weighing approximately 6,000,000 kg, and estimated to be 80,000 years old.
The world's heaviest twins were Billy Leon and Benny Loyd McCrary (USA), who together weighed 743 kg (1,637 lbs) and performed as professional wrestlers.

The fastest land speed record is 1,227.985 km/h (763.035 mph), set by Andy Green of the UK in the Thrust SSC jet-powered car in Black Rock Desert, Nevada on October 15, 1997—the only supersonic land speed record.
The world's most lightning-struck place is the Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, which experiences around 1.2 million lightning strikes per year—earning it the nickname 'the everlasting storm.'
The longest recorded punt in NFL history was 98 yards (89.6 meters), kicked by Steve O'Neal of the New York Jets against the Denver Broncos on September 21, 1969.
The world record for the most simultaneous skydivers in formation was 400, achieved by an international team over Udon Thani, Thailand on February 9, 2006.
The most expensive book ever sold at auction was the Codex Leicester by Leonardo da Vinci, purchased by Bill Gates for $30.8 million at Christie's in 1994.
The world's fastest typist achieved 216 words per minute using a QWERTY keyboard, set by Stella Pajunas-Garnand of the USA in 1946—a record that stood for decades.
The world's most visited tourist attraction is the Eiffel Tower in Paris, which has welcomed over 300 million visitors since its opening in 1889.
The world's driest place outside Antarctica is the Atacama Desert in Chile, where some weather stations have never recorded any rainfall.
The fastest land speed record on a bicycle is 280.57 km/h (174.33 mph), set by Denise Mueller-Korenek of the USA at the Bonneville Salt Flats in 2018 while being paced by a dragster.
The world's most goals scored by a goalkeeper in a career was Rogerio Ceni of Brazil, who scored 131 goals (from free kicks and penalties) for São Paulo FC from 1990 to 2015.

The most children born to one woman in history was reportedly 69 children by the wife of an 18th-century Russian peasant, Feodor Vassilyev, including 16 pairs of twins, 7 sets of triplets, and 4 sets of quadruplets.
The longest running theatrical show in history is The Mousetrap by Agatha Christie, which has been performed continuously in London's West End since 1952, with over 28,000 performances.
The highest ever recorded air temperature on the surface of a planet in our solar system is approximately 465°C (869°F) on Venus, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun.
The world's most expensive commercial airline seat is Emirates' A380 First Class Private Suite at around $21,000 for a one-way flight from London to Dubai.
The world's fastest growing tree is the Empress tree (Paulownia tomentosa), which can grow up to 6 meters (20 ft) in its first year under ideal conditions.
The world's longest suspension bridge by main span is the Çanakkale 1915 Bridge in Turkey, completed in 2022 with a main span of 2,023 meters, surpassing the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge.

source.name: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat

text: The world's most runs scored in a single cricket innings is 501 not out, by Hanif Mohammad of Pakistan against Bahawalpur in a first-class match in 1958–59.
The heaviest edible mushroom in Guinness World Records was a giant puffball (Calvatia gigantea) found in 1992 in Canada that weighed 26 kg (57 lbs) and measured 2.64 meters in circumference.
The fastest time a human has descended Mount Everest was 10 hours and 56 minutes for the entire ascent to Everest summit in the record by Pemba Dorje Sherpa in 2004.
The world's tallest statue is the Statue of Unity in Gujarat, India, depicting Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel; it stands 182 meters (597 ft) tall, nearly twice the height of the Statue of Liberty.
The oldest Olympic Games records that still stand are from the 1960 Summer Olympics; Livio Berruti's 200-meter time of 20.5 seconds held as an Olympic record for years.
The most World Series titles in baseball history are held by the New York Yankees with 27 championships, far more than any other Major League Baseball franchise.
The world's longest golf hole is the 964-meter (1,054-yard) par-7 seventh hole at Sano Course in Japan's Satsuki Golf Club.
The highest ever temperature recorded on Mars was 35°C (95°F) on the surface during summer at the equator, while lows can reach -125°C (-193°F) at the poles.
The world's rarest blood type is Rh-null (known as 'golden blood'), with fewer than 50 people worldwide known to have it; it can be given to anyone with Rh disease.
The world record for the tallest stack of pancakes measures 101.8 cm (3 ft 4 in) and was achieved by Dean Kassaby in Leicester, UK in 2016.
The oldest fossil of a complex animal is a 558-million-year-old specimen of Dickinsonia found in Russia, confirmed by cholesterol analysis to be an animal and not a plant or fungus.
The fastest completion of the Marathon des Sables—a 250-km, six-stage ultramarathon through the Sahara—was 16 hours 22 minutes and 29 seconds by Rachid El Morabity of Morocco in 2018.

The world's most powerful telescope is the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, which can observe objects over 13.6 billion light-years away—seeing the universe as it was less than 300 million years after the Big Bang.
The most expensive publicly accessible toilets in the world are the ones in the Lobster Bar & Grill in Hong Kong, encrusted with semi-precious stones and valued at over $3.5 million.
The world's record for the longest time driving nonstop was achieved by Claudia Mori of Italy, who drove for 86 hours and 13 minutes (without sleeping) in 2005.
The world's fastest human-made object was the Parker Solar Probe, which reached a speed of 635,266 km/h (394,736 mph) as it swung around the Sun in November 2021.
The world's most expensive burger sold commercially is the FleurBurger 5000 at Fleur restaurant in Las Vegas at $5,000, featuring Wagyu beef, foie gras, and black truffle sauce.
The largest simultaneous fireworks display involved 810,904 fireworks detonated over 5 sites in the UAE on January 1, 2014, in celebration of the New Year.

The world's largest natural arch is Landscape Arch in Arches National Park, Utah, spanning 88 meters (290 ft) wide—longer than a football field—and is just 1.8 meters (6 ft) thick at its thinnest point.
The world record for number of skips on water by a stone is 88, achieved by Kurt Steiner of the USA on September 6, 2013, at Red Bridge in Pennsylvania.
The most goals scored in a single NHL season was 92, by Wayne Gretzky of the Edmonton Oilers in the 1981–82 season—a record considered unbreakable in the modern era.
The largest hailstone ever officially recorded in the United States fell in Vivian, South Dakota on July 23, 2010, measuring 20.3 cm (8 in) in diameter and weighing 879 grams.
The longest continuous wall painting in the world measures 5,000 meters (5 km) in length and was completed in Maharashtra, India in 2022.
The world's loudest recorded thunder clap was estimated at 186 decibels, experienced by a crew near Belo Horizonte, Brazil in 2001—more than double the volume that can cause immediate hearing damage.
The world record for the most consecutive free throw attempts made is 5,221, set by Ted St. Martin of the USA in 1996.
The most number of countries visited in 24 hours is 13, achieved by Babis Bizas of Greece in 1999, entering 13 different nations in a single day while traveling through Europe.

The world's tallest structure is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai at 828 meters, but the Jeddah Tower in Saudi Arabia, currently under construction, is designed to surpass 1,000 meters — the first structure ever planned to exceed one kilometer in height.

source.name: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat

text: The world's widest building is the New Century Global Centre in Chengdu, China, completed in 2013; it covers a floor area of 1.76 million square meters — roughly three times the size of the Pentagon — and houses a hotel, shopping malls, a water park, and an IMAX cinema.

The world's longest cantilever bridge is the Quebec Bridge in Canada, completed in 1917 after two catastrophic collapses during construction that killed 88 workers; its main span measures 549 meters and was the longest of any type when built.

The deepest artificial excavation ever made is the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, drilled between 1970 and 1994 to a depth of 12,262 meters; at that depth, temperatures reached 180°C — far hotter than predicted — and the drill bit effectively melted, forcing the project to stop.

The largest palace in the world is the Forbidden City (Palace Museum) in Beijing, China, covering 720,000 square meters and containing 9,999 rooms across 980 buildings; it was constructed between 1406 and 1420 and served as China's imperial seat for nearly 500 years.

The world's largest dam by volume of material used is the Tarbela Dam in Pakistan on the Indus River, containing 138.6 million cubic meters of fill; the Three Gorges Dam in China, though larger in power output, contains far less material by volume.

The world's tallest statue is the Statue of Unity in Gujarat, India, depicting the independence leader Vallabhbhai Patel; completed in 2018, it stands 182 meters tall — nearly twice the height of the Statue of Liberty — and required 210,000 cubic meters of concrete to build.

The world's longest arch bridge is the Chaotianmen Bridge over the Yangtze River in Chongqing, China, with a main span of 552 meters; it carries both road and rail traffic on separate decks and was completed in 2009.

text: The tallest wooden structure in the world is the Mjøstårnet tower in Brumunddal, Norway, completed in 2019 at 85.4 meters; it is built from engineered mass timber (cross-laminated timber) and demonstrates that wood can compete with steel and concrete for multi-storey construction.

text: The world's largest single-roof structure is the Aerium hangar in Brand, Germany, a former Soviet airship hangar 360 meters long, 210 meters wide, and 107 meters tall; it is so large that it has its own weather system and indoor clouds can form near the ceiling.

The Voyager spacecraft holds the computing record for distance: Voyager 1's onboard computer has 69.63 kilobytes of memory — less than a cheap pocket calculator — yet has operated continuously for over 45 years and transmits scientific data from beyond our solar system.

The world's most powerful supercomputer (as of 2024) is Frontier at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the USA, achieving 1.1 exaFLOPS — 1.1 quintillion floating-point calculations per second — making it the first supercomputer to break the exascale barrier.

The world's largest computer hard drive shipped commercially is Seagate's HAMR (Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording) drive at 32 terabytes per platter; a single rack of these drives can store more information than all words ever spoken by humanity.

The world's fastest internet speed ever recorded was 301 terabits per second (Tbit/s), achieved by UK and Japanese researchers in 2024 using a single optical fibre — enough bandwidth to download the entire Netflix library every second.

The world's fastest chess player is Magnus Carlsen of Norway, who achieved a FIDE bullet chess (1 minute per side) rating of 3385 in 2024 — the highest ever recorded — making him statistically the greatest bullet chess player in history.
The best-selling video game of all time is Minecraft, published by Mojang/Microsoft, with over 300 million copies sold across all platforms as of 2024; it surpassed Tetris to claim the title in 2019.

The world's largest music event by attendance was the Rod Stewart free concert on Copacabana Beach, Rio de Janeiro on New Year's Eve 1994, drawing an estimated 3.5 million people — the largest crowd ever assembled for a single musical performance.

The best-selling music album of all time is Michael Jackson's Thriller (1982), with estimated sales of 66–100 million copies worldwide; it spent 37 weeks at number one and holds the record for most weeks on the US Billboard 200 chart by any album.

The longest recorded note held by a human voice was 41.5 seconds, achieved by Antonio Sabato Jr.'s vocal coach Enrico Caruso at a public performance in 1910 — though modern records show soprano Vesna Zornik holding a note for 56.23 seconds in 2023.

The most Grammy Awards won by an individual is 32 by Beyoncé, achieved with her 2024 album Cowboy Carter; she surpassed Georg Solti's record of 31 wins and became the most decorated Grammy artist in the award's history.

The world's most expensive musical instrument is the 'Lady Blunt' Stradivarius violin, made in 1721 by Antonio Stradivari, which sold for $15.9 million in 2011; Stradivarius instruments are prized for their unparalleled tonal quality, though scientists still debate the exact reason for their superiority.

The best-selling book of all time (excluding religious texts) is Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes, published in two parts (1605 and 1615), with an estimated 500 million copies sold; it is also considered the first modern European novel.

The longest novel ever written is À la recherche du temps perdu (In Search of Lost Time) by Marcel Proust, comprising 7 volumes and approximately 1.5 million words; reading it at an average pace would take about 350 hours of continuous reading.

The most translated book in history is the Bible, which has been translated in whole or in part into 3,589 languages as of 2023; the New Testament alone exists in 1,658 languages, making it the most linguistically accessible text in human history.

The fastest-selling book series in history is J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter; Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (2007) sold 11 million copies in the first 24 hours in the US and UK alone, setting a record that has never been surpassed.

The world's most expensive scientific experiment is the International Space Station, which has cost approximately $150 billion to build and operate since 1998, with contributions from 15 nations; it is continuously crewed and serves as a laboratory for research that cannot be done on Earth.

The world's most powerful particle accelerator is the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, which accelerates protons to 99.9999991% the speed of light; the collision energies of 13.6 TeV achieved in 2022 allowed discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 and set multiple particle physics records.

The coldest temperature ever achieved by scientists is 38 picokelvins (38 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero), reached in 2021 using magnetic-field-cooled atomic gas aboard the International Space Station, surpassing any temperature achievable on Earth.

The highest temperature ever created by humans is approximately 9.9 trillion degrees Fahrenheit (5.5 trillion °C) — 250,000 times hotter than the Sun's core — achieved in 2012 by the ALICE experiment at CERN when gold nuclei collided at near-light speed.

The world's largest telescope is the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), currently under construction in Australia and South Africa, which will use thousands of radio antennas to collect data across a total area of one square kilometre; when complete it will be 50 times more sensitive than any existing radio telescope.

The longest continuous scientific experiment is the pitch drop experiment at the University of Queensland, Australia, started in 1927 by Professor Thomas Parnell; only nine drops of pitch have fallen in nearly 100 years, and no one has ever seen a drop actually fall.

The world's largest pizza delivery was a 13,580.7 sq ft gluten-free pizza made in Rome in 2012 that was subsequently cut into 98,000 slices and delivered to food banks — combining a world record with charitable work.

The most expensive spice in the world by weight is saffron, derived from the stigmas of Crocus sativus flowers; it takes approximately 150,000 flowers handpicked over three weeks to produce 1 kg of saffron, explaining its current retail price of $5,000–$10,000 per kg.

The world's most expensive coffee is Kopi Luwak, made from coffee beans that have been eaten and excreted by Asian palm civets; genuine wild-sourced Kopi Luwak sells for up to $700 per kg, though 'farmed' versions are widely sold as fraudulent substitutes.

The world's largest food fight is the La Tomatina festival in Buñol, Spain, held annually on the last Wednesday of August; around 20,000 participants throw approximately 150,000 kg of overripe tomatoes at each other in an hour-long battle.

The world record for eating hot dogs is 76 hot dogs in 10 minutes, set by Joey 'Jaws' Chestnut at the Nathan's Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest on July 4, 2021; Chestnut has won the contest 16 times, making him the most dominant competitive eater in the event's history.

The highest Olympic medal tally per capita by country is held by Finland, which has won over 300 Olympic medals for a population of 5.5 million; the country's dominance in cross-country skiing, athletics, and long-distance running reflects its outdoor sporting culture.

Kenya has produced more male 1500m and marathon world record holders than any other nation; the Kalenjin people from the Rift Valley, representing less than 0.06% of world population, have won approximately 40% of all major distance running titles since the 1960s.

Jamaica has the best record of any nation in the 100m and 200m Olympic sprints relative to population; with under 3 million people, Jamaica has produced Usain Bolt, Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, and Elaine Thompson-Herah, dominating sprinting at the highest level for two decades.

The United States has won more total Olympic medals (over 2,600) than any other nation in Summer Olympic history; it leads in gold medals (over 1,000) as well, with particular strength in swimming, athletics, basketball, and gymnastics.

Fauja Singh became the first centenarian to complete a full marathon when he finished the Toronto Waterfront Marathon on October 16, 2011, at age 100 in 8 hours, 11 minutes, and 6 seconds; he took up running at age 89 after the death of his son.

The oldest person to climb Mount Everest was Yuichiro Miura of Japan, who reached the summit on May 23, 2013, at age 80 years and 224 days; Miura had previously summited at ages 70 and 75, defying the limit of human endurance at extreme altitude.

The world record for the oldest marathon runner is set by Fauja Singh at 101 years old in 2012 (Toronto Marathon); however, Ed Whitlock of Canada ran a sub-4-hour marathon at age 73 and a sub-4.5-hour marathon at age 85, representing the longest sustained marathon performance relative to age.

Jeanne Calment's age of 122 years and 164 days remains unverified by some demographers due to gaps in early records, but is accepted by Guinness World Records; the second-oldest verified person ever was Kane Tanaka of Japan, who died in April 2022 at 119 years and 107 days.

The world record for the most tattoos on the body belongs to Lucky Diamond Rich of Australia (born Gregory McLaren), who has 100% of his skin tattooed, including the insides of his eyelids, mouth, ears, and foreskin, using many layers of ink — the latest in white over black over coloured over black original tattoos.

The world's largest collection of rubber ducks belongs to Charlotte Lee of the USA, who has amassed over 9,000 different rubber duck designs; Guinness World Records recognizes her as holding the largest collection, which she started in 1996.

The largest collection of Star Wars memorabilia belongs to Steve Sansweet of the USA (a former Lucasfilm director), who amassed over 500,000 items at his 'Rancho Obi-Wan' museum in California — requiring a dedicated museum barn to house the collection.

The largest Lego set ever produced is the Lego Titanic (set 10294), released in 2021, containing 9,090 pieces and measuring 135.6 cm when assembled — the longest Lego set ever made, requiring an average of 16–17 hours to complete.

The world marathon record progression shows the two-hour barrier was broken by Eliud Kipchoge on October 12, 2019, at 1:59:40.2 in Vienna — though this is not an official world record because it used pacemaking teams; his official WR is 2:00:35 from the 2023 Berlin Marathon.

The women's marathon world record is 2:09:56, set by Tigst Assefa of Ethiopia at the 2023 Berlin Marathon, improving the previous record by over 2 minutes — the largest improvement to the women's marathon record in decades.

The Boston Marathon, held annually since 1897, is the world's oldest annual marathon; it was the first marathon to officially include women's divisions (1972) and has been run over 125 consecutive times, making it the longest continuously-held marathon in history.

Yuki Kawauchi of Japan is the only person in modern history to have run more than 100 sub-2:20 marathons; he is also a full-time civil servant who trains without a professional coach, making him the world's fastest 'amateur' elite marathoner.

The longest distance run in 24 hours (road course) is 303.5 km, set by Aleksandr Sorokin of Lithuania in 2022; the distance covered in 24 hours — like running seven consecutive marathons — represents the pinnacle of ultra-endurance athletic performance.

The greatest distance swum nonstop is 225.3 km, achieved by Croatian swimmer Veljko Rogošić across Lake Garda in 50 hours and 10 minutes in 2006; the record has stood for nearly 20 years, demonstrating the extraordinary limits of long-distance swimming.

The longest distance cycled in one year is 139,399 km, set by Kurt Searvogel of the USA in 2015; cycling an average of 382 km per day — roughly nine times the average daily cycling distance of a Tour de France rider — for an entire year.

The deepest point ever reached by a human in a submarine is 10,928 meters in Challenger Deep, Mariana Trench, achieved by James Cameron in his Deepsea Challenger solo submarine in March 2012; the dive took 2 hours 36 minutes to descend and 70 minutes to ascend.

The deepest mine in the world is the Mponeng Gold Mine in South Africa at 4,000 meters below the surface; at that depth, temperatures reach 66°C and the mine requires massive refrigeration systems and ice-slurry pumped down to keep working conditions survivable.

The world's highest altitude city where people permanently reside is La Rinconada in Peru, at 5,100 meters above sea level; residents live with approximately 50% the oxygen available at sea level, and the city, which has a population of around 30,000 gold miners, has no running water or sanitation.

The highest structure ever built by humans was the Warszawa Radio Mast in Poland, which reached 646.38 meters; it was the world's tallest structure from 1974 until it collapsed during maintenance in 1991, when workers accidentally allowed a supporting cable to go slack.

The world record for the most weight lifted in competition is 484 kg total (snatch + clean and jerk) in the super-heavyweight category, set by Georgian weightlifter Lasha Talakhadze at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics; he set world records in all three disciplines at those Games.

The heaviest pumpkin ever recorded weighed 1,247.9 kg (2,750 lbs 12.9 oz), grown by Travis Gienger of the USA and verified at the 2023 World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, California; giant pumpkins grow at an average of 18 kg per day at peak growth.

The world record for the shortest time to shear a sheep is 39.31 seconds, set by Ivan Scott of Northern Ireland in 2016; professional sheep shearers like New Zealand's champion shearers can shear over 800 sheep in a working day — a rate of one sheep every 90 seconds.

The longest-running TV show in the world is NBC's Meet the Press, which premiered in November 1947 and has aired continuously for over 77 years; the Simpsons holds the record for the longest-running animated TV show at over 35 seasons.

The world record for the most people simultaneously playing the same song on guitar is 7,411, achieved at a Nirvana-themed event in Wrocław, Poland in 2009; participants played 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' in unison in a concert hall and public spaces across the city.

The largest human gathering in history was the Kumbh Mela in Allahabad (Prayagraj), India, in January–February 2013, when an estimated 30 million people gathered in a single day — the largest crowd ever assembled for any purpose on Earth.

The world's longest handshake endurance record is 43 hours, 35 minutes and 17 seconds, set by Alastair Galpin and Craig Rofe of New Zealand in 2011; both participants had to keep continuous palm-to-palm contact for the duration, requiring extreme concentration.

The record for the most hours spent in space by a single person is held by Oleg Kononenko of Russia, who surpassed 878 days in space in February 2024 — more than 2.4 years living in microgravity, requiring extensive rehabilitation for bone density and muscle mass recovery.

The world record for holding one's breath underwater (static apnoea) is 24 minutes and 37 seconds, achieved by Aleix Segura Vendrell of Spain on February 28, 2016; competitive freedivers train by inducing physiological changes including a diving reflex that slows heart rate to under 10 beats per minute.

The deepest free dive (constant ballast) is 122 meters, held by Alexey Molchanov of Russia as of 2023; freedivers at this depth experience a 'lung pack' where air is absorbed into blood vessels, allowing them to survive pressures that would crush a rigid-walled vessel.

The world's largest parade of classic cars is the Speedweek parade in Goodwood, UK, where over 600 vintage racing cars drive in a moving festival of automotive history; however, the longest car parade ever recorded featured 4,645 Mustangs driving in convoy in Tennessee in 2018.

The longest winning streak in professional sports belongs to the Hungarian women's water polo team, which won 99 consecutive international matches between 1985 and 1992; the team's dominance was so complete that international opponents often withdrew rather than face certain defeat.

The world's longest winning streak in any major team sport belongs to the New Zealand All Blacks rugby union team, who won 18 consecutive tests in 2013–2014; however, the Leinster Province rugby team won 25 consecutive Heineken Cup matches from 2012 to 2013.

The world's most simultaneous skydivers in formation was 400, achieved by an international team over Perris Valley, California on September 26, 2006; the formation — a flat 'flower' shape — required all 400 jumpers to exit multiple planes and join the formation within just 4.25 seconds at 6,100 meters altitude.

The world's largest natural pearl is the Pearl of Puerto (also called the Pearl of Allah), measuring 24 cm in diameter and weighing 6.4 kg; found in 1934 in a giant clam off Palawan, Philippines, it was valued at $93 million in 2016.

The world's fastest typist was Stella Pajunas, who typed 216 words per minute on an IBM electric typewriter in 1946; the modern keyboard record is 212 WPM achieved by Anthony Ermolin on a standard QWERTY keyboard in 2022.

The fastest time to solve a Rubik's Cube (3x3x3) was achieved by Max Park of the USA in 3.13 seconds at the Pride in Long Beach 2023 competition; the average fastest solve over multiple attempts is 4.48 seconds, with cubers analyzing cube states in under 0.3 seconds before executing up to 7 moves per second.

The most expensive painting ever sold at auction is Leonardo da Vinci's Salvator Mundi, which fetched $450.3 million at Christie's New York in November 2017; the work depicts Christ as 'Saviour of the World' and was purchased by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

The world's largest sculpture by volume is the Crazy Horse Memorial in South Dakota, USA, being carved from a 172-meter-high granite mountain; started in 1948 by Korczak Ziolkowski to honor the Lakota leader, it is still under construction after 75 years and will be larger than Mount Rushmore when complete.

The world's largest aquarium (by water volume) is the Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, USA, containing 10.3 million gallons (39 million liters) of fresh and salt water and housing 120,000 animals of 700 species including whale sharks — the largest fish in the world.

The highest altitude marathon is the Everest Marathon (EBM) in Nepal, starting near Everest Base Camp at 5,364 meters and finishing in Namche Bazar at 3,446 meters; runners must acclimatize for 3 weeks before the race and the winning time is typically over 3 hours 40 minutes due to altitude effects.

The coldest permanent settlement on Earth is Oymyakon in Yakutia, Russia, which recorded a low of −67.7°C (−89.9°F) in February 1933; the approximately 500 residents must plug their cars in every night and schools only close when temperatures fall below −55°C.

The most venomous animal on Earth is the box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri), whose venom is so powerful that it can kill a human in under 5 minutes; the jellyfish has 24 eyes (one for each tentacle cluster), although its brainless body cannot process the images they capture.

The world's smallest country by area is Vatican City at 0.44 km², with a population of around 800 people; it also holds the record for the highest crime rate per capita in the world (mainly pickpocketing and theft by visitors), as most Vatican 'residents' are clergy with diplomatic immunity.

The world's largest diamond ever found is the Cullinan Diamond, unearthed in South Africa in 1905, weighing 3,106.75 carats (621.35 g); it was cut into 105 stones, with the two largest — the Great Star of Africa and the Lesser Star of Africa — forming part of the British Crown Jewels.

The world's most simultaneous jigsaw puzzle builders set a record at the German Games Prize 2009 in Frankfurt, with 1,544 people working on a single 1,000-piece puzzle simultaneously; competitive puzzle solving now has its own World Jigsaw Puzzle Championship.

The most tennis Grand Slam singles titles ever won is 24, held by Novak Djokovic of Serbia; he leads Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal (20 titles each) and is the first man to win each Grand Slam tournament at least three times.

The world record for the most wickets taken in Test cricket is held by Muttiah Muralitharan of Sri Lanka, who took 800 wickets in 133 Tests (1992–2010); his unique 'doosra' and off-spin deliveries, bowled with a controversial but ICC-approved bowling action, confounded batsmen worldwide.

Lionel Messi holds the record for the most Ballon d'Or awards with 8 (as of 2023), the prestigious annual honour given to the world's best footballer; he has won the award in 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2019, 2021, and 2023.

The world's highest batting average in Test cricket is 99.94, held by Australian Don Bradman; statisticians calculate that had Bradman scored just 4 runs in his final innings (he was dismissed for 0), he would have retired with an average of exactly 100.

The world record for the most ascents of Mount Everest is held by Kami Rita Sherpa of Nepal, who summited for the 29th time in May 2024; the Sherpa people from Nepal's Solukhumbu district have collectively climbed Everest more times than all non-Sherpa climbers combined.

The record for the longest time spent underground in isolation was set by Béatrice de Géa (Project Olo) in 2023, who spent 500 days alone in a 100-meter-deep cave in France without daylight, clocks, or contact with the outside world to study time perception and human physiology.

The most NBA championships won by a team is 17, tied between the Boston Celtics and the Los Angeles Lakers; the Celtics won their 17th NBA title in 2024, ending a tie that had stood since the Lakers' last championship in 2020.

The oldest continuous government on Earth is the Papal States / Vatican City, claiming institutional continuity from the Apostolic succession of the 1st century CE; the San Marino republic, founded in 301 CE, is more reliably the world's oldest republic — it has had an elected government continuously since 1243 CE.

The world's most visited museum is the Louvre in Paris, which received 8.9 million visitors in 2023 after a post-pandemic recovery; the museum's collection contains over 480,000 works, of which only 35,000 are displayed, and is so large that visiting every exhibit for 30 seconds would take over 100 days.

The world record for the highest base jump is from a hot air balloon at 40,000 feet (12,192 meters) in 2012 by Felix Baumgartner, who exited over 39,000 meters for his Red Bull Stratos jump — actually becoming the first human to break the sound barrier without a vehicle, reaching Mach 1.25 (1,357.64 km/h).

The most goals scored in a single FIFA World Cup tournament is 13 by Just Fontaine of France at the 1958 World Cup in Sweden — a record that has stood for over 65 years and is widely considered the most unassailable record in international football.

The world's most expensive privately-owned home is Antilia in Mumbai, India, owned by Mukesh Ambani; the 27-floor skyscraper serves as a private residence for the billionaire's family and their 600 full-time staff, and is valued at approximately $2 billion.

The world record for the most minutes of music released in a single day by one artist is 18 hours by DJ and producer Aphex Twin, who uploaded 100 tracks to SoundCloud simultaneously in 2014, though this unofficial record was exceeded when Taylor Swift released all 10 songs from Midnights plus three bonus tracks simultaneously in October 2022, occupying the top 13 spots on the Hot 100.

The fastest human-powered vehicle on record is a recumbent bicycle (HPV) designed by Todd Reichert and the Aerovelo team; their bike AeroVelo Eta reached 144.17 km/h (89.59 mph) on September 18, 2016, at Battle Mountain, Nevada — faster than most motorcycles on ordinary roads.

The world's largest chocolate bar weighed 5,792.5 kg and was made by Thorntons in Derbyshire, UK on October 7, 2011; it was 4 meters long and 4 meters wide, beating the previous record by nearly 2 tonnes and taking 24 hours to make.

The world record for the fastest speed in a road race motorcycle (MotoGP) is 366.1 km/h (227.5 mph), set by Ducati rider Pecco Bagnaia during qualifying at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix at Mugello — a track known for its long straight that allows maximum speed.

The record for most medals at a single Summer Olympics by an individual is 8, achieved by Michael Phelps at the 2008 Beijing Games; in total he won 28 Olympic medals (23 gold) across four Olympics — the most medals ever won by any Olympic athlete in history.

The world record for the most Olympic gold medals by a gymnast is 7, held by Larisa Latynina of the Soviet Union across the 1956, 1960, and 1964 Olympics; she also holds the overall record for most Olympic medals by a gymnast at 18 (9 gold, 5 silver, 4 bronze).

The world record for the most points scored in an NBA game by a single player is 100, set by Wilt Chamberlain of the Philadelphia Warriors on March 2, 1962, against the New York Knicks; no player has come close since, with the second-highest single-game score being 81 by Kobe Bryant in 2006.

The most World Cups won by a national football team is 5, held by Brazil; the Seleção has won in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002, and is the only team to have participated in every FIFA World Cup since the tournament's inception in 1930.

The world record for the longest successful field goal in NFL history is 66 yards, kicked by Brett Maher of the Dallas Cowboys on December 11, 2022; the longest field goal attempt ever made was 76 yards by Sebastian Janikowski in 2011, which was short.

The world's fastest land animal record, the cheetah's 112 km/h, was scientifically measured in 2012 using GPS tracking on a wild cheetah named Sarah at the Cincinnati Zoo; previous estimates relied on mechanical timing and may have underestimated the true peak speed.

The fastest insect on record is the male horsefly (Hybomitra hinei wrighti), which can reach 145.8 km/h (90.6 mph) while pursuing females in flight — faster than a cheetah — as recorded in a 2008 study using high-speed photography.

The world's fastest bird in level flight is the common swift, which has been recorded at 111.6 km/h — faster than any other bird in horizontal flight — and spends up to 10 months of the year airborne, landing only to nest.

The world's loudest animal relative to body size is the water boatman insect (Micronecta scholtzi), which produces sounds of up to 99.2 decibels — as loud as a passing freight train — by rubbing its penis against its abdomen; the insect itself is only 2mm long.

The world's largest living reptile is the saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), with the largest on record measuring 6.17 meters and weighing over 1,000 kg; they can live to 70+ years and survive saltwater, freshwater, and brackish environments across the Indo-Pacific.

The world record for the largest litter of domestic cats from a single birth was 19 kittens (of which 15 survived) born to a Burmese-Siamese cat named Tarawood Antigone in 1970; the Guinness Book verified this as it was delivered by caesarean section under veterinary supervision.

The most expensive cow ever sold at auction was a Canadian Holstein named Missy, which sold for $1.2 million in 2009; dairy cattle breeding records are regularly broken as high-producing genetics command enormous premiums in the global cattle industry.

The world's deepest lake is Lake Baikal in Siberia, Russia, at 1,642 meters deep; it contains approximately 20% of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water — more than all five of North America's Great Lakes combined — and is estimated to be 25–30 million years old, making it also the world's oldest lake.

The world's tallest tree is a coast redwood named Hyperion in Redwood National Park, California, at 115.7 meters (380 feet) — taller than St. Paul's Cathedral in London; its exact location is kept secret by the National Park Service to prevent damage from visitors.

The world's most expensive natural disaster in US history was Hurricane Katrina (2005), causing $186 billion in damage (2023 dollars); however, in terms of insurance claims adjusted for inflation, Hurricane Ian (2022) at $112 billion was the costliest Florida storm ever.

text: The world record for the most languages spoken fluently by an individual belongs to Ziad Fazah of Lebanon, who claimed to speak 58 languages; more conservatively, Alexander Arguelles is documented speaking 50+ languages with varying proficiency, considered the modern standard for hyperpolyglots.

The world record for the fastest a human has ever solved Pi calculations is held by Emma Haruka Iwao of Google Japan, who calculated Pi to 100 trillion decimal places in 2022, using Google Cloud over 157 days and producing a number so large that if printed in standard font it would extend roughly 400 trillion centimetres.

The world's longest-lasting light bulb is the Centennial Light at Livermore, California's Fire Station 6, which has been burning almost continuously since 1901; as of 2024 it is over 123 years old, earning it certification by Guinness World Records as the oldest burning light bulb.

The world record for the largest simultaneous snowball fight involved 9,127 participants in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Canada on January 31, 2016; participants were organized in two teams and hurled snowballs for three minutes in −20°C temperatures.

The world's most-streamed artist in Spotify history (as of 2024) is Drake, whose songs and albums have accumulated over 75 billion streams; he held the record for most-streamed artist for multiple years before being overtaken by Taylor Swift in daily streams in 2023.

The most watched YouTube video of all time is 'Baby Shark Dance' by Pinkfong, which has over 14 billion views as of 2024 — more than double the Earth's population; it surpassed 'Despacito' as the most-viewed video in 2020 after only being posted in 2016.

The world's most expensive photograph ever sold at auction is 'Rhein II' (1999) by Andreas Gursky, which sold for $4.3 million at Christie's in 2011; the large-format print of the River Rhine digitally edited to remove power station and path is considered a masterpiece of contemporary photography.

The world record for the most skips (double unders) in one minute using a jump rope is 233, achieved by Jordan Rapp of the USA in 2021; competitive jump rope athletes can complete up to 280 rotations per minute in speed events.
The world record for the most push-ups in 24 hours is 46,001, set by Charles Servizio of the USA in 1993 — averaging over 530 push-ups per hour, every hour, continuously for a full day.

The world record for the most pull-ups in one hour is 1,009, achieved by Jan Kares of the Czech Republic in 2022; he averaged approximately 16.8 pull-ups per minute for 60 continuous minutes without letting go of the bar.

The world's most complex clock is the Jens Olsen World Clock in Copenhagen City Hall, built between 1945 and 1955 with 14,000 parts, 70 dials, and 12 movements; it simultaneously shows solar time, local time, star time, the Julian calendar, and the positions of celestial bodies.

The world's most accurate atomic clock is the optical lattice clock developed at NIST and the University of Colorado, which loses or gains only one second every 300 billion years — roughly 22 times the current age of the universe — making it the most precise measurement instrument ever built.

The world's largest hotel is the Venetian in Las Vegas, which together with the Palazzo has over 7,000 suites; however, the Izmailovo Hotel in Moscow has the most rooms at 7,500, while the First World Hotel in Malaysia (with 7,350 rooms) holds the Guinness record for most rooms in a single structure.

The world's longest river cruise is the Yangtze River route from Wuhan to Chongqing in China, which passes through the Three Gorges; however, the world's longest ocean cruise was offered by Viking in 2023 — a 245-day World Cruise visiting 65 countries on 7 continents starting at $50,000 per person.

The world's smallest country by population is Vatican City with approximately 800 residents, but the smallest by land area with an internationally recognized sovereign government is Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, whose permanent population has dropped as low as 42 people.

The most followers ever accumulated on a social media platform by a single account was held by @cristiano (Cristiano Ronaldo) on Instagram with over 630 million followers as of 2024 — making his social media audience larger than the population of the United States and EU combined.

The longest continuous chain of paper clips was 2,179,049 links (approximately 46 km), assembled by students at a school in Lapua, Finland in 2022; paper clip chain records are a popular fundraising activity, with many towns and schools attempting to break the community record.

The world's most expensive spice — saffron — is also involved in the world's most expensive dish: the 'Zillion Dollar Lobster Frittata' at Le Parker Meridien Hotel in New York, which costs $1,000 and includes a whole lobster, 10 oz of caviar, and saffron.

The world record for the most Michelin stars held by a single chef was 21, previously held by Joël Robuchon of France across his global restaurant empire before his death in 2018; Alain Ducasse currently holds the record for most stars of any living chef at 19 across his restaurants.

The most tennis aces served in a single Grand Slam match was 113, by Ivo Karlović of Croatia in a 6-hour Wimbledon match in 2012; Karlović holds the record for most career aces served in professional tennis at over 13,700, leveraging his 6ft 6in frame and 240 km/h serves.

The world's oldest marathon — the Marathon, Greece race held annually since 1972 — follows the mythological route of Pheidippides; however, the Athens Classic Marathon (since 490 BCE in legend and since 1896 in practice) follows the actual ancient battle route, making it the world's longest-running marathon tradition.

The world record for the longest winning streak in a sport by a single athlete is held by Ric Flair, who won 57 consecutive professional wrestling matches between 1971 and 1979 — though as professional wrestling is staged entertainment, the real-sport equivalent is table tennis player Jan-Ove Waldner's 34-match winning streak in competitive tournaments.

The world's largest parade ever recorded was India's Republic Day parade in New Delhi on January 26, 2023, with over 1 million people watching along Kartavya Path; the parade route was extended by nearly 3 km and lasted over 4 hours.

The world's fastest elevator is in the Shanghai Tower (Shanghai), reaching speeds of 20.5 meters per second (73.8 km/h), travelling from the 2nd floor to the 119th in just 55 seconds; it uses aerodynamic car bodies and regenerative braking to handle its velocity without discomfort.

The world's largest shopping mall by total area is the New South China Mall in Dongguan, China, with a gross leasable area of 892,000 square meters and capacity for over 2,350 stores; despite its size, it has remained mostly empty (over 99% vacant) since opening in 2005, earning the nickname 'the world's largest ghost mall.'

The world record for the largest human mosaic (using people forming an image) was achieved in the Philippines in 2012, when 30,000 people assembled in Pasay City to form the image of a Philippine flag; human mosaic records require precise coordination of participants wearing coloured costumes.

The most siblings to run a marathon simultaneously is 22, achieved by the Gooch family in the UK during the 2018 London Marathon; the oldest sibling was 68 and the youngest was 22, and the entire family finished within a 5-hour window.

The world's most successful horse in history is Winx, an Australian Thoroughbred mare who won 33 consecutive Group 1 races between 2015 and 2019 — the longest winning streak at the highest level in the sport's history, earning over AUD $26 million in prize money.

The fastest 400-metre hurdles times were both set in Tokyo: Karsten Warholm of Norway ran 45.94 seconds (men's WR, 2021) and Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone of the USA ran 50.65 seconds (women's WR, 2022) — both times represented improvements of over half a second on previous records, unprecedented in 400m hurdles history.

The world record for the most complex domino toppling structure was a 600,000-piece domino cascade built by German domino artists Sinners Domino Entertainment in 2020, creating a 3-D sculptural display that took 23 people 15 days to set up and 10 minutes to topple.

The world record for the fastest circumnavigation of Earth on foot was set by Jean-Louis Étienne of France, who walked 24,901 miles (40,075 km) — the circumference of the Earth at the equator — in 225 days; the Guinness-verified running circumnavigation record belongs to Robert Garside, who ran 35,000 km in about 6 years.

The most goals scored in a professional football career is attributed to Romário of Brazil, who claimed 1,000 goals (though not all are verified); FIFA and Guinness World Records officially credit Josef Bican of Austria/Czechoslovakia with 805 verified goals in competitive football — more than Pelé (765) or Ronaldo (900+, including friendlies).

The world's tallest sandcastle was built in Blokhus, Denmark, in July 2021; the structure reached 21.16 meters — taller than a four-storey building — using 4,860 tonnes of sand and a team of 30 sand sculptors working for 6 weeks.

The world's largest choir performance was 121,440 singers performing simultaneously at 'The Spirit of Harmony Foundation' world record event in Hyderabad, India in 2011; every participant sang the same song simultaneously, which was verified by Guinness World Records officials.

The most wins at the Tour de France is 7, held jointly by Lance Armstrong (stripped of all titles due to doping) and new record holder Eddy Merckx (5 wins); based on verified results, Merckx, Jacques Anquetil, Bernard Hinault, and Miguel Indurain each hold the verified record of 5 Tour de France victories.

The world's smallest commercially available computer is the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, measuring just 65mm × 30mm and costing $15; smaller experimental computers have been built in laboratories, including IBM's 1mm³ computer (2018) that is smaller than a grain of salt but can perform basic functions.

The world's most downloaded app of all time is TikTok, which reached 4 billion total downloads in 2022 across iOS and Android platforms; it surpassed WhatsApp and Facebook in 2020 and now has over 1.5 billion monthly active users.

The world record for the most national championships won in any team sport is held by Real Madrid FC in football (soccer), who have won the Spanish La Liga 36 times and the UEFA Champions League/European Cup a record 15 times as of 2024.

The world record for the highest paid single-season contract in Major League Baseball is $50 million per year, held by Shohei Ohtani's 10-year, $700 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers signed in December 2023 — the largest contract in North American professional sports history.

The world's largest ball of twine is a subject of competing claims: the largest publicly acknowledged one is in Cawker City, Kansas, now over 20,100 pounds (9,100 kg), which is open for visitors to add to; Frank Stoeber started it in 1953 and it has grown continuously ever since.

The world's most expensive car ever sold at auction was a 1955 Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé, which sold for €135 million ($143 million) in a private sale by Sotheby's in May 2022 — replacing the previous record holder, a Ferrari 250 GTO (sold for $70 million in 2018).

The world record for the fastest 100m butterfly in swimming (long course) is 49.45 seconds, set by Caeleb Dressel of the USA at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics; Dressel won 5 gold medals at those Games, matching Michael Phelps' record at a single Olympics for American swimmers.

The record for the most Wimbledon titles in women's singles is 9, held by Martina Navratilova of Czechoslovakia/USA (1978–1990); she also holds the record for most total Grand Slam titles in women's singles at 18, tied with Chris Evert and Steffi Graf.

The world's highest poker winnings in a single tournament is $20.5 million, won by Daniel Negreanu's poker-room competitor Bryn Kenney at the 2019 Big One for One Drop at the WSOP; the World Series of Poker main event has had prize pools exceeding $80 million.

The world's most expensive perfume by volume is Clive Christian No. 1 Pure Perfume, retailing at £175,000 ($215,000) per 30ml bottle, made with extracts including Tahitian vanilla, Indian sandalwood, and Tonkin musk; each bottle is set in 18-carat gold with a diamond-set top.

The world record for the most lightning strikes survived is 7, by American park ranger Roy Sullivan between 1942 and 1977; his hair was set on fire twice and he lost a toenail, suffered burns to shoulders, chest, stomach, and ankle, and eventually took his own life — unrelated to the strikes.

The world record for the most goals scored in a single FIFA World Cup (total by all teams) was at France 1998, which produced 171 goals across 64 matches — the most goals ever scored in a single tournament before the introduction of VAR reduced goal counts in later editions.

The world's highest-altitude lake accessible by road is Ojos del Salado crater lake at 6,390 meters above sea level in the Andes on the Chile-Argentina border; it exists within the crater of the world's highest active volcano and is only accessible to experienced mountain climbers.

The world's most expensive watch ever sold at auction is the Patek Philippe Grandmaster Chime Ref. 6300A, which fetched CHF 31.19 million ($31.2 million) at Christie's Geneva in 2019; the stainless steel watch was the first Patek Philippe ever made in steel with this movement, made exclusively for a charity auction.

The world's longest confirmed sniper kill (after Guinness verification) is 3,540 metres by a Canadian soldier in Iraq using a McMillan TAC-50 in 2017; the bullet took approximately 10 seconds to reach its target, and the shooter had to account for Earth's rotation (Coriolis effect) when aiming.

The world record for the most expensive bottle of wine ever sold at auction is a 1945 Romanée-Conti Burgundy, which fetched $558,000 at Sotheby's New York in October 2018; there are only three bottles of this wine known to exist.

The world's largest collection of stamps belongs to Iqbal Mirza of Pakistan, who had over 8 million stamps verified by Guinness World Records in 2010; the global philately market is valued at over $10 billion, with the rarest stamps fetching millions at auction.

The world's most-climbed mountain (by guided clients per year) is not Everest but Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, which receives approximately 50,000 climbers annually; it is accessible to non-technical climbers but has a summit success rate of only about 65% due to altitude sickness.

The loudest concert ever recorded was a KISS performance in Ottawa, Canada in 2009, which measured 136 dB at the mixing desk 50 meters from the stage; exposure to that sound level for more than one second can cause permanent hearing damage.

The most days spent on the summit of Mount Everest by a single person is 10, by Kami Rita Sherpa; beyond their record number of ascents, Sherpa guides have collectively spent more time on Everest's peak than all other climbers combined, often making multiple trips in a single season.

The world's largest crop field of a single species is the winter wheat fields of the Russian Stavropol Krai region, a single contiguous agricultural zone covering over 2.3 million hectares; such monocultures are both productivity records and ecological vulnerabilities to disease.

The world's fastest animal striker is the mantis shrimp, whose club appendage accelerates at 10,000 g to strike at 23 meters per second; the impact creates cavitation bubbles that implode with a force nearly equal to a .22 calibre bullet, allowing the shrimp to break crab shells and aquarium glass.

The world's most popular video game franchise is Pokemon, which has sold over 480 million video games, 43.2 billion trading cards, and generated over $150 billion in total franchise revenue since 1996 — more than any other media franchise in history.

The world's most expensive commercial satellite is NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, which cost $10 billion and took over 20 years to build; it can observe galaxies 13.6 billion light-years away, effectively seeing the universe as it existed just 200 million years after the Big Bang.

The world's largest collection of comics belongs to Bob Bretall of California, USA, who had verified ownership of 101,822 unique comic books as of 2014; his collection occupies 3,500 linear feet of shelving and requires a dedicated climate-controlled room in his house.

The fastest human ever on water skis was clocked at 247 km/h (153.5 mph), achieved by Jeret 'Speedy' Peterson on a specially designed 'straight skis' course in Sacramento, California in 2009; this exceeds the top speed of many motorboats used recreationally.

The world's most visited website is Google.com, receiving approximately 89 billion visits per month (2023 data); the runner-up is YouTube, which receives 75 billion monthly visits — both owned by Alphabet Inc., which collectively controls the world's two most-visited web properties.

The record for the most Nobel Prizes won by a country is held by the United States with 403 individual American Nobel laureates as of 2024 — far ahead of the UK (138) and Germany (115); this dominance reflects America's large research university and corporate R&D system.
